chapter: The Mathematics of Maybe: Introduction to Probability (Class 9 Maths)
note: 50 mixed-form items across the chapter's concepts. Difficulty 17 Easy / 17 Medium / 16 Hard.

items.stem: The probability of any event always lies between
items.explanation: A probability cannot be negative and cannot exceed certainty, so it lies from 0 to 1 inclusive.

options.why: A negative probability has no meaning.
That is the range as a percentage, not as a probability.
No probability can exceed 1, which is certainty.

items.stem: An event that is certain to happen has probability
items.explanation: Certainty is the top of the scale and corresponds to a probability of 1.

options.why: Zero is the probability of an impossible event.
A half describes an event as likely as not.
100 is the percentage form; as a probability it is 1.

items.stem: The number of outcomes in the sample space for one throw of a fair die is
items.explanation: A standard die can land on any of six faces, so the sample space has six outcomes.

options.why: Two outcomes describe a coin, not a die.
Twelve would be the count for two dice, not one.
Thirty-six is the sample space for two dice thrown together.

items.stem: The probability of getting a head when a fair coin is tossed once is
items.explanation: One of two equally likely outcomes is a head, so the probability is one half.

options.why: A quarter would apply to two heads in two tosses.
A head is not certain; a tail is equally possible.
A head is possible, so its probability is not zero.

items.stem: A die is thrown once. The probability of getting an even number is
items.explanation: Three of the six faces are even, so the probability is three sixths, that is one half.

options.why: A third would require only two favourable faces.
A sixth is the probability of one particular face.
Two thirds would require four favourable faces.

items.stem: Experimental probability is calculated as
items.explanation: It is the number of times the event occurred divided by the total number of trials performed.

options.why: That gives the odds, not the probability.
This inverts the ratio and can exceed one.

options.text: favourable outcomes divided by all outcomes
options.why: That is the theoretical probability, not the experimental one.

items.stem: A coin is tossed 200 times and gives 108 heads. The relative frequency of a head is
items.explanation: The relative frequency is 108 divided by 200, which is 0.54.

options.why: That is the theoretical value, not what this experiment gave.
This divides the trials by the successes, inverting the ratio.
This is the raw count, not a relative frequency.

items.stem: A fair coin has landed heads five times running. The probability that the next toss is a head is
items.explanation: Tosses are independent, so the coin has no memory of previous results and the probability stays one half.

options.why: This is the gambler's fallacy; a fair coin does not compensate for past results.
Past heads do not make the coin more likely to give heads.
Independence means the run has no bearing on the next toss.

items.stem: As the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends to
items.explanation: The law of large numbers says the relative frequency settles towards the theoretical probability as trials increase.

options.text: move away from the theoretical value
options.why: Increasing trials reduces rather than increases the discrepancy.
It approaches the true probability, which need not be one half.

options.text: stay fixed at the first result
options.why: Further trials continually revise the relative frequency.

items.stem: A die is described as biased. This means that
items.explanation: A biased die does not give every face an equal chance, so the theoretical equally likely model does not apply.

options.text: its faces are not equally likely
it has more than six faces
options.why: Bias is about the chances, not the number of faces.

options.text: it can never show a six
options.why: Bias makes some faces less likely, not impossible.

options.text: its probabilities do not sum to one
options.why: The probabilities of all outcomes always sum to one, biased or not.

items.stem: What does probability measure?
items.answer: Probability measures how likely an event is to happen, on a scale from 0 for impossible to 1 for certain.

items.stem: What is the sample space of an experiment?
items.answer: The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of the experiment. For a single coin toss it is head and tail.

items.stem: What makes an experiment random?
items.answer: An experiment is random when its individual outcome cannot be predicted in advance, even though all the possible outcomes are known and their long-run pattern is predictable.

items.stem: A die is thrown. Write the event of getting a number greater than 4.
items.answer: The event is the set containing 5 and 6, which has two outcomes, so its probability is two sixths, that is one third.

items.stem: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue balls. Find the probability of drawing a red ball.
items.answer: There are 8 balls in all and 3 of them are red, so the probability is 3 by 8.

items.stem: If the probability of an event is 0.3, what is the probability that it does not happen?
items.answer: 0.7, because an event and its complement together are certain, so their probabilities add to 1.

items.stem: Why can experimental probability differ from theoretical probability?
items.answer: Theoretical probability describes the long-run proportion under an ideal model, while an experiment is a finite number of trials subject to chance variation. With few trials the observed proportion can differ considerably, and only as the number of trials grows does it settle towards the theoretical value.

items.stem: A die gives 30 sixes in 60 throws. Is it necessarily biased?
items.answer: It is strong evidence of bias, since 30 sixes is far above the expected 10, but no finite experiment proves bias with certainty. The right conclusion is that bias is very likely and should be tested with more throws.

items.stem: Explain the difference between theoretical and experimental probability, with an example of each.
items.answer: Theoretical probability is worked out from the structure of the experiment by counting favourable outcomes and dividing by the total number of equally likely outcomes. For a fair die the theoretical probability of a six is one sixth. Experimental probability is worked out from what actually happened, by dividing the number of times the event occurred by the number of trials. If a die is thrown 60 times and gives 12 sixes, the experimental probability is 12 by 60, that is one fifth. The theoretical value never changes, while the experimental value changes with every new set of trials, and the two come closer together as the number of trials increases.

items.stem: Write the sample space for tossing two coins together, and find the probability of getting exactly one head.
items.answer: Listing by the outcome of the first coin then the second, the sample space is HH, HT, TH and TT, so there are four equally likely outcomes. Exactly one head occurs in HT and TH, which is two of the four outcomes. So the probability is two quarters, that is one half. It is worth noting that HT and TH must be counted separately; treating one head as a single outcome would wrongly give one third.

items.stem: A bag contains 5 red, 4 green and 6 yellow balls. One ball is drawn at random. Find the probability that it is (a) green, (b) not yellow.
items.answer: The total number of balls is 5 plus 4 plus 6, which is 15. (a) Four balls are green, so the probability of green is 4 by 15. (b) Six balls are yellow, so nine are not yellow, giving a probability of 9 by 15, which simplifies to 3 by 5. Alternatively, the probability of yellow is 6 by 15, that is 2 by 5, and subtracting from 1 gives 3 by 5, which agrees.

items.stem: Use a tree diagram to find the probability of getting two heads when a coin is tossed twice.
items.answer: The first stage of the tree has two branches, H and T, each with probability one half. From each of those, a second stage has two branches, H and T, again each with probability one half. This gives four complete paths: HH, HT, TH and TT. Multiplying along the HH path gives one half times one half, which is one quarter. So the probability of two heads is one quarter. As a check, the four paths have probabilities one quarter each and they add to 1, as they must, since one of the four outcomes is certain to occur.

items.stem: A die is thrown 120 times and a six appears 24 times. Compare the experimental and theoretical probabilities.
items.answer: The experimental probability is 24 divided by 120, which is 0.2 or one fifth. The theoretical probability for a fair die is one sixth, about 0.167. The experimental value is higher, by about 0.033. That difference is not large for 120 trials and is well within what ordinary chance variation could produce, so this result gives no strong reason to doubt that the die is fair. To decide the question one would throw the die many more times and see whether the relative frequency settles near one sixth or stays near one fifth.

items.stem: Explain the law of large numbers and what it does and does not promise.
items.answer: The law of large numbers says that as the number of trials of a random experiment increases, the relative frequency of an event tends towards its theoretical probability. If a fair coin is tossed a thousand times, the proportion of heads will usually be close to one half, and closer still after ten thousand tosses. What the law does not promise is anything about the raw counts or about any particular trial. It does not say the number of heads and tails will become equal, and in fact the absolute difference between them typically grows even as the proportion settles. It says nothing about the next toss, which remains one half whatever has gone before. Confusing the proportion settling with the counts evening out is exactly the mistake behind the gambler's fallacy.

items.stem: A player argues that after four tails a head is due. Explain why this reasoning fails.
items.answer: The reasoning treats the coin as if it remembered its previous results and adjusted to compensate, which it cannot do. Each toss is independent: the physical coin has no record of the past, so the probability of a head remains one half on every toss regardless of what preceded it. The player is misapplying the law of large numbers, which says that the proportion of heads approaches one half over many tosses, and reading it as a promise that the counts will even out soon. They do not; the proportion approaches one half because the number of tosses grows, not because later tosses are adjusted. This mistake is called the gambler's fallacy, and it is the reason a run of losses gives no reason to expect a win. The only situation where the reasoning would have force is drawing without replacement, where earlier draws genuinely change what remains.

items.stem: How would you investigate whether a coin is fair, and what would make your conclusion trustworthy?
items.answer: Toss the coin a large number of times under consistent conditions, recording each result, and compute the running relative frequency of heads. A fair coin should give a relative frequency settling near 0.5 as the number of tosses grows. To make the conclusion trustworthy, several things matter. The number of tosses must be large, since a short run tells almost nothing: eight heads in ten tosses is unremarkable for a fair coin. The tossing method must not itself favour a side, so the coin should be spun or flipped high and caught or allowed to land, not placed. All results must be recorded, including any the experimenter dislikes, as discarding results is how bias enters the data rather than the coin. Finally the conclusion should be stated with its limits: a relative frequency near 0.5 over ten thousand tosses is good evidence of fairness, but it is evidence rather than proof, since no finite experiment can rule out a very small bias.

items.stem: Assertion (A): No probability can be greater than 1. Reason (R): A probability of 1 means the event is certain. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and since certainty is the most that can be said of an event, nothing can exceed it.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Certainty being the maximum is precisely why 1 is the ceiling.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: A probability of 1 does mean the event is certain.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: A probability above 1 would mean more than certain, which is meaningless.

items.stem: Assertion (A): After three heads, a tail is more likely. Reason (R): Coin tosses are independent events. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true and is exactly what defeats the assertion: independence means the past cannot affect the next toss.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Independence rules out the compensation the assertion assumes.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: Coin tosses genuinely are independent, so the reason is true.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: The probability stays one half after any run of results.

items.stem: Assertion (A): In many tosses the number of heads and tails becomes equal. Reason (R): The relative frequency of heads approaches one half. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: the proportion settles while the absolute difference in counts typically grows.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: A settling proportion does not force the raw counts to match.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: The relative frequency genuinely does approach one half.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: The gap between the counts typically widens even as the ratio settles.

items.stem: Assertion (A): An experimental probability of 0 proves the event is impossible. Reason (R): Probability 0 denotes an impossible event. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: an event may simply not have occurred in the trials performed, which is not the same as being impossible.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: Not occurring in a finite run does not make an event impossible.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: A theoretical probability of 0 does denote impossibility.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Ten throws of a die may give no six, yet a six is clearly possible.

items.stem: State whether true or false: the probability of an impossible event is 0.
items.explanation: Zero is the bottom of the probability scale and denotes impossibility.

options.why: An event that cannot occur has probability exactly 0.

items.stem: State whether true or false: the probabilities of all outcomes of an experiment add up to 1.
items.explanation: One of the outcomes is certain to occur, so their probabilities must total 1.

options.why: Since some outcome must occur, the total probability is exactly 1.

items.stem: State whether true or false: a random experiment has outcomes that cannot be listed in advance.
items.explanation: The possible outcomes are known and can be listed; it is which one occurs that cannot be predicted.

options.why: The sample space is known in advance; only the particular result is unpredictable.

items.stem: State whether true or false: drawing cards without replacement makes successive draws independent.
items.explanation: Removing a card changes what remains, so later probabilities depend on earlier draws and the events are dependent.

options.why: Without replacement each draw changes the pack, making the draws dependent.

items.stem: The probability of a certain event is ___________.
The set of all possible outcomes of an experiment is called the ___________.
items.answer: sample space

items.stem: If the probability of rain is 0.4, the probability of no rain is ___________.
The probability of drawing a king from a full pack of 52 cards is ___________.
items.answer: 4 by 52, which simplifies to 1 by 13

items.stem: Explain the basic vocabulary of probability: experiment, outcome, sample space, event and probability.
items.answer: A random experiment is an action whose result cannot be predicted in advance, such as tossing a coin or throwing a die. Each possible result is an outcome; for a die the outcomes are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes, so for a die it has six members and for a coin it has two. An event is any collection of outcomes that we are interested in, such as getting an even number, which is the set containing 2, 4 and 6. The probability of an event, when all outcomes are equally likely, is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the number in the sample space; for an even number on a die this is 3 divided by 6, that is one half. Probability is measured on a scale from 0 to 1, where 0 means impossible and 1 means certain, and the probabilities of all the outcomes in the sample space always add to 1.

items.stem: A coin is tossed and a die is thrown. Use a tree diagram to find the probability of a head and a number greater than 4.
items.answer: The first stage of the tree is the coin, with two branches, H and T, each of probability one half. From each of these the second stage is the die, with six branches numbered 1 to 6, each of probability one sixth. That gives twelve complete paths in all, and since the coin and die are independent, the probability of each path is one half times one sixth, which is one twelfth. The event we want is a head together with a 5 or a 6, which corresponds to the paths H5 and H6. Two paths at one twelfth each give a total probability of two twelfths, that is one sixth. As a check, there are twelve equally likely paths and two of them are favourable, which again gives 2 by 12, or one sixth. The tree diagram is useful here because it keeps the two stages separate and shows clearly that the number of outcomes multiplies rather than adds.

items.stem: Describe an experiment to demonstrate the law of large numbers, including what you would record and what you would expect to see.
items.answer: Toss a fair coin repeatedly, recording each result in order, and after every ten tosses calculate the running relative frequency of heads, that is the total heads so far divided by the total tosses so far. Continue to at least five hundred tosses. Plot the running relative frequency against the number of tosses. What to expect: at the start the graph swings widely, and after ten tosses a value of 0.3 or 0.7 would be unremarkable. As the number of tosses grows the swings become smaller and the graph settles into a narrow band around 0.5, without ever locking exactly onto it. Two features are worth recording deliberately. First, the settling is in the proportion, not the counts: the difference between the number of heads and the number of tails usually grows larger as the experiment continues, even while the ratio narrows. Second, no individual toss is affected by the trend; a run of five heads can appear at any point, including late in the experiment. Together these show what the law actually claims, and guard against reading it as a promise that the counts will even out.

items.stem: Discuss the ways probability is commonly misunderstood in everyday reasoning.
items.answer: The first and commonest error is the gambler's fallacy, the belief that a run of one result makes the opposite result due. Independent trials have no memory, so the probability is unchanged by the past, and the law of large numbers concerns the proportion rather than the counts. The second is treating a small sample as decisive. Eight heads in ten tosses feels remarkable but happens often with a fair coin, and a conclusion drawn from ten trials is worth very little. The third is confusing probability with certainty in a single case: a forecast of a 90 per cent chance of no rain is not falsified by one wet day, since the claim was about the long-run proportion of such days. The fourth is ignoring the difference between drawing with and without replacement; without replacement earlier draws genuinely change the later probabilities, and applying the independent model there gives wrong answers. The fifth is selective recording, where results that fit an expectation are remembered and the rest forgotten, which makes almost any belief look confirmed. The common thread is that probability makes claims about patterns across many trials, and each of these errors comes from reading such a claim as a statement about one particular trial.

items.stem: A bag contains 4 white and 6 black balls. Find the probability of drawing a white ball.
items.answer: The total number of balls is 4 plus 6, which is 10. Four of them are white, so the probability is 4 by 10, which simplifies to 2 by 5, that is 0.4.

items.stem: In 500 tosses of a coin, a head appeared 265 times. Find the relative frequency of a head and of a tail.
items.answer: The relative frequency of a head is 265 divided by 500, which is 0.53. The number of tails is 500 minus 265, which is 235, so the relative frequency of a tail is 235 divided by 500, which is 0.47. The two add to 1.00, as they must, since every toss gives one or the other.

items.stem: Two dice are thrown together. Find the probability that the sum of the numbers is 8.
items.answer: Each die has 6 faces, so the sample space has 6 times 6, that is 36 equally likely outcomes, counting the dice as distinguishable. The pairs giving a sum of 8 are (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3) and (6,2), which is five outcomes. Note that (2,6) and (6,2) are counted separately because they are different outcomes of the two dice, while (4,4) occurs only once. So the probability is 5 by 36. A useful check is that sums from 2 to 12 have frequencies 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2, 1, which total 36; the sum of 8 sits at the fifth position from the top end, giving 5, which agrees.

items.stem: Match each event in Column I with its probability in Column II. Column I: (a) a tossed coin shows a head, (b) a die shows 7, (c) a die shows a number below 7, (d) a die shows 3. Column II: (i) 0, (ii) one sixth, (iii) one half, (iv) 1.
items.answer: (a) a head - (iii) one half, since one of two equally likely outcomes. (b) a die shows 7 - (i) 0, since it is impossible. (c) below 7 - (iv) 1, since it is certain. (d) a die shows 3 - (ii) one sixth, one favourable face of six.

items.stem: Match each experiment in Column I with the size of its sample space in Column II. Column I: (a) one coin, (b) two coins, (c) one die, (d) two dice. Column II: (i) 6, (ii) 36, (iii) 2, (iv) 4.
items.answer: (a) one coin - (iii) 2, being head and tail. (b) two coins - (iv) 4, being HH, HT, TH and TT. (c) one die - (i) 6, one for each face. (d) two dice - (ii) 36, being 6 times 6.

items.stem: Draw a labelled tree diagram for tossing a coin three times and use it to find the probability of exactly two heads.
items.answer: Draw a first branching point with two branches labelled H and T, each marked with probability one half. From each of those two endpoints draw another pair of branches labelled H and T, again each one half, giving four endpoints. From each of those four draw a final pair of branches, giving eight endpoints in total. Label each complete path along the way: HHH, HHT, HTH, HTT, THH, THT, TTH, TTT. Mark each path with its probability, obtained by multiplying one half three times, which is one eighth. Check on the diagram that the eight probabilities add to 1. Now ring the paths with exactly two heads: HHT, HTH and THH. That is three paths, each of probability one eighth, so the probability of exactly two heads is 3 by 8. Annotate the diagram to note that exactly two heads is not the same as at least two heads, which would also include HHH and so give 4 by 8.

items.stem: Sketch and annotate a graph of running relative frequency against number of trials for a fair coin, and mark what it shows.
items.answer: Draw axes with the number of tosses on the horizontal axis, from 0 to about 500, and the relative frequency of heads on the vertical axis, from 0 to 1. Draw a horizontal dashed line at 0.5 and label it theoretical probability. Now sketch a curve that begins with large swings near the left of the graph, reaching values such as 0.3 and 0.8 within the first twenty tosses, and that gradually narrows as it moves right, settling into a band close to the dashed line by the right-hand end without ever sitting exactly on it. Annotate three features. First, label the wide left-hand region small samples are unreliable, since a few tosses can give almost any proportion. Second, label the narrowing convergence towards the theoretical probability, and note that this is the law of large numbers. Third, add a note that the curve narrows but never becomes flat, because every further toss still changes the running total slightly, and add a warning label that the raw difference between heads and tails generally grows even as this curve settles, so the graph shows the ratio converging and not the counts evening out.

items.stem: Prove that the probability of an event and the probability that it does not happen always add to 1.
items.answer: Let the experiment have a sample space S consisting of n equally likely outcomes, and let E be an event consisting of m of those outcomes, where m is between 0 and n. The event that E does not happen, written not E and called the complement of E, consists of exactly the outcomes of S that are not in E. Since every outcome of S either is in E or is not, and none can be both, the outcomes split into these two groups with no overlap and nothing left over. So the number of outcomes in not E is n minus m. Now compute the two probabilities. By definition P(E) equals m divided by n, and P(not E) equals (n minus m) divided by n. Adding them gives m over n plus (n minus m) over n, which is (m plus n minus m) over n, that is n over n, which equals 1. Hence P(E) plus P(not E) equals 1, and rearranging gives the useful form P(not E) equals 1 minus P(E). Two remarks. First, the argument used only that the two groups are exhaustive and do not overlap, so it holds for any sample space, not merely an equally likely one. Second, the rearranged form is often the quickest route to an answer: the probability of at least one head in three tosses is easiest found as 1 minus the probability of no heads, which is 1 minus one eighth, that is seven eighths.
